title: ExecutorOwner: back la_avdecc executor with libdispatch serial queue
body:
Swap the underlying la_avdecc executor from ExecutorWithDispatchQueue (one dedicated std::thread + condvar per EndStation) to ExecutorProxy backed by a libdispatch serial queue. Each EndStation now shares the libdispatch global worker pool instead of holding its own kernel thread, which is the main reason for the change.

Implementation notes:

- pushJob/flush/terminate map onto dispatch_async / dispatch_sync; the serial queue gives the FIFO ordering the Executor interface promises.
- Producers and flush/terminate are serialised by enqueueLock so a pushJob racing with terminate(flushJobs=true) cannot land a stray block onto the queue after the drain has returned.
- A queue-specific key lets flush()/terminate()/close() detect a recursive call from a job and skip the dispatch_sync drain that would otherwise self-deadlock.
- close() does the drain itself before dropping the wrapper, since ExecutorProxyImpl's destructor is a no-op (unlike ExecutorWithDispatchQueueImpl's), and reset()-from-close would otherwise leave queued blocks running against torn-down captures.
- getExecutorThread() returns std::thread::id{}. libdispatch does not pin a serial queue to a fixed kernel thread, and ExecutorManager snapshots the value once at registration anyway, so a per-job cache would not be consulted later. Returning {} disables the inline short-circuit in waitJobResponse / runJobOnExecutorAndWait so those always take the queued-and-wait path. The single resulting constraint is documented in the class comment: a Swift handler running on this executor must not synchronously call a la_avdecc API that internally posts a job to the same executor and waits on it.

On Darwin the queue is created with QOS_CLASS_USER_INITIATED, matching the prior ThreadPriority::Highest intent. swift-corelibs-libdispatch on Linux does not ship the QOS_CLASS_* enum, so we fall back to a plain serial queue (inherits caller priority).
